title: NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check codes now reach encoding rates up to 50% at useful distances. Their checks however are long-range group actions, not local neighbourhoods, and that connectivity has so far been supplied by neutral atoms. Silicon spin qubits offer the same primitive --- coherent transport of qubit blocks --- through electron shuttling, and on microsecond rather than millisecond timescales. They however travel along fabricated tracks rather than free space: permutations an atom array obtains by moving tweezers must here become collision-free motions on a physical lattice. We here present the first code and spin-qubit hardware co-design. We build an architecture whose geometry mimics that of a family of non-abelian groups, broad enough to host codes of excellent parameters: a hierarchy of nested conveyor-belt loops on a plain square lattice of shuttling tracks, in which every group multiplication becomes a rigid, globally controlled motion of whole qubit trains. We call it NeST, for Nested Shuttling Tracks. A code search over the family returns rate-20% mitten codes up to $[[1400,280,\leq 28]]$, and circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing give thresholds above $10^{-3}$ with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles, two to three orders of magnitude faster than neutral-atom implementations. Via extrapolations, we estimate that this largest code may reach a logical error probability per qubit per round of $10^{-14}$, assuming a ten-fold improvement on early shuttling demonstrations, with other physical errors at p=0.1%. Logic is compatible with NeST too: for the [[150,30,10]] code we build a code-surgery gadget in which every qubit again moves only by rigid belt motions, at no qubit cost and a 29% increase in gate layers. This demonstrates that ultra-low-overhead fault tolerance and a fast clock speed are not competing goals, and that silicon spin qubits can supply both.
summary: This paper presents NeST, a novel hardware architecture for silicon spin qubits that implements high-rate quantum error-correcting codes. By mapping code structure onto nested shuttling tracks mimicking group theory, it achieves significantly faster stabilizer cycles than previous platforms. This work proves that high performance and fault tolerance can coexist in solid-state quantum computing.
main_problem: The challenge is to build quantum error correction codes (qLDPC) with high encoding rates that are physically realizable on solid-state hardware, overcoming limitations in connectivity and speed.
main_result: The authors introduce NeST, an architecture using silicon spin qubits, which enables high-rate codes with sub-50us stabilizer cycles, demonstrating that fast clock speeds and low-overhead fault tolerance are compatible.
method: The work involves co-designing the quantum code structure (based on group theory) with the hardware geometry (nested conveyor-belt loops) and simulating performance under realistic noise models.
model_or_system: The physical system is silicon spin qubits utilizing electron shuttling along fabricated tracks. The architecture, NeST, mimics the geometry of non-abelian groups, allowing group multiplication to be realized as rigid, global motions of qubit trains.
key_observables: Logical error probability ($P_L$), stabilizer cycle time (sub-50us), code rate (up to 20-30%), and circuit distance ($d_{	ext{circ}}$).
important_parameters: Shuttling dephasing rate ($	ext{psh}$), physical error rates ($p$), and the required group structure parameters ($\vec{n}, \sigma$).
main_assumptions: The core primitive is collision-free, rigid, global motion of qubit trains along a plain lattice of shuttling tracks.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the NeST architecture mapping code blocks onto the lattice and show simulations comparing logical error rates under spin-specific noise versus depolarizing noise.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical limitations and proposing the NeST architecture via group theory, to simulating high-rate codes, and finally evaluating performance under detailed noise models, including gadget construction for fault tolerance.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, hardware-aware roadmap for fault-tolerant quantum computation using solid-state qubits, directly addressing the engineering bottleneck of scaling QEC codes.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A lifted product code on the NeST architecture. (a) The five data qubit blocks of a mitten code — four left blocks (corners) and one right block (centre) — become five unit cells on a single square lattice of shuttling tracks, arranged in the 2D pattern of the protograph. Each cell holds |G| static data qubits and can host one block of shuttled ancillas at a time. Within a cell, ancillas move as described in Fig. 4; between cells they are translated wholesale along the inter-cell highways (dark purple, arrows), which supply the long-range connectivity the base matrices A and B may demand. The pale tracks are optional: the lattice is strictly square throughout and may be made denser...

FIG. 2. Cyclic group embedding on a conveyor loop. A single loop with n = 4 sites, drawn before (left) and after (right) the multiplication by r3. The data qubits (circles) are static and label the sites of the loop by the group elements r0, . . . , r3; the ancillas (squares) ride the belt and are labelled by the element they carry. Advancing the belt by three sites sends the ancilla rj from site rj to site rj+3, leaving every data qubit where it is. Thus a multiplication by rk is realised by one global rotation of the belt, meaning that the shuttling control cost is independent of n.
FIG. 3. Shuttling-track embedding of the group G = Cn1 ⋊−1 Cn2. Each one of the n2 tier-1 loops hosts n1 data qubits (yellow circles) labelled as the elements rksl of Cn1sl

(a) Initial config- uration: ancilla and data labels are aligned. (b) Intra-loop rotation: each hosting loop rotates its n1 ancillas collectively along its belt. Same-colour loops always follow the same rela- tive rotation direction, but different-colour loops alternatively co- or counter-rotate (left or right multiplication by a rota- tion). (a) Four tier-2 cells (n3 = 4), each of them a copy of Fig. 3 (up to a few new non-optional tracks), are arranged as a 2 × (n3/2) array and connected by tier-3 tracks (pink). Here ⃗n = (4, 6, 4). Left/right and top/bottom cells are spaced by 6 and 2n2 −1 edges respectively, chosen so that the trains of panel (b) never meet.
